people.name: Didius Julianus
people.summary: Wealthy Milanese senator raised in Marcus Aurelius' household who bought the throne from the Praetorians on 28 March 193 and was killed in the palace on 1 June after 66 days, as Severus approached Rome.
people.death: killed in the palace on the Senate's order, 1 June 193

people.name: Septimius Severus
people.summary: African senator from Lepcis Magna (born 11 April 145) who won the civil wars of 193-197, sacked Ctesiphon, created the province of Mesopotamia and founded the Severan dynasty; he died campaigning in Britain.
people.detail: Severus spoke Latin with an African accent and had Punic-speaking relatives. His reign raised army pay, enlarged the garrison of Rome, gave equestrians new commands (the Parthian legions, Mesopotamia), and saw the classic age of Roman jurisprudence under Papinian, Ulpian and Paul. His second wife Julia Domna of Emesa, chosen, it was said, because her horoscope promised she would marry a king, presided over an intellectual circle. Gibbon called him the principal author of the decline of the empire; modern assessments (Birley) emphasise his administrative competence and the continuity of his government.
people.death: illness at Eboracum, 4 February 211

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Birley, Septimius Severus: The African Emperor (1971, 2nd ed. 1988)

people.name: Pescennius Niger
people.summary: Italian equestrian-born senator and governor of Syria proclaimed emperor in April 193; popular in Rome but slow to act, he was defeated at Cyzicus, Nicaea and Issus and killed fleeing toward Parthia.
people.death: caught and beheaded near Antioch, 194

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Clodius Albinus
people.summary: Aristocrat from Hadrumetum, governor of Britain, who accepted the rank of Caesar from Severus in 193, proclaimed himself Augustus when sidelined, and died after the battle of Lugdunum.
people.death: killed or suicide after the battle of Lugdunum, 19 February 197; his corpse was trampled by Severus' horse

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Julia Domna
people.summary: Daughter of the high priest of Elagabal at Emesa, wife of Septimius Severus and mother of Caracalla and Geta, honoured as 'mater castrorum et senatus et patriae'; she patronised a circle of intellectuals including Philostratus, whom she commissioned to write the Life of Apollonius of Tyana.
people.detail: She handled petitions and correspondence for Caracalla and was in Antioch when he was murdered. Her sister Julia Maesa and nieces Soaemias and Mamaea carried the dynasty on through Elagabalus and Severus Alexander, the most politically powerful set of women in Roman imperial history.
people.death: starved herself to death at Antioch after Caracalla's murder, 217

people.name: Caracalla
people.fullName: Marcus Aurelius Severus Antoninus (born Lucius Septimius Bassianus)
people.summary: Elder son of Severus, nicknamed after the Gallic hooded cloak he favoured; he murdered his brother Geta, issued the Constitutio Antoniniana (212), introduced the antoninianus, built the great baths and was assassinated near Carrhae during a Parthian war.
people.detail: Caracalla cultivated the soldiers, raising their pay by half, and modelled himself on Alexander the Great, raising a Macedonian phalanx. Dio, who knew him, portrays a paranoid, cruel ruler; his massacre at Alexandria and purge after Geta's murder confirm the brutality. His portraits, with a scowling turn of the head, deliberately projected menace.
people.death: assassinated by Julius Martialis near Carrhae, 8 April 217

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Geta
people.summary: Younger son of Severus, joint emperor with Caracalla from 211; murdered by his brother in their mother's arms in December 211 and subjected to one of the most thorough damnationes memoriae known.
people.death: murdered on Caracalla's orders in the palace, December 211

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Plautianus
people.summary: Fellow Lepcitane and perhaps kinsman of Severus, praetorian prefect with near-total power, father-in-law of Caracalla; he was killed in the palace in January 205 after a probably fabricated plot charge.
people.death: killed in the palace, 22 January 205

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Papinian
people.summary: Regarded by later Romans as the greatest of the jurists; author of Quaestiones and Responsa, prefect under Severus, executed by Caracalla in 212, according to tradition for refusing to justify the murder of Geta.
people.detail: The Law of Citations of 426 made Papinian the decider when other authorities were evenly split. Justinian's law students in their third year were called 'Papinianistae'.
people.death: executed on Caracalla's orders, 212

people.name: Ulpian
people.summary: Jurist from Tyre whose vast output (commentaries Ad Edictum, Ad Sabinum) supplied about one-third of Justinian's Digest; as Severus Alexander's praetorian prefect he was murdered by the Praetorians.
people.detail: His definitions (justice as 'constans et perpetua voluntas ius suum cuique tribuendi'; the distinction of public and private law; the emperor 'legibus solutus') shaped European legal thought.
people.death: murdered by Praetorians in the palace, probably 223
scholarship: Honoré, Ulpian: Pioneer of Human Rights (2nd ed. 2002)

people.name: Cassius Dio

roles.t: Governor of Africa, Dalmatia and Pannonia Superior

people.summary: Senator from Nicaea whose 80-book Greek Roman History, from Aeneas to 229, is a contemporary witness for Commodus and the Severans, surviving for this period mainly in Byzantine epitomes.
scholarship: Millar, A Study of Cassius Dio (1964)

people.name: Herodian
people.summary: Greek historian, probably from the East and of modest official rank, whose eight books cover 180-238; vivid and moralising but chronologically vague, he is the main narrative source for 235-238.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Kemezis, Greek Narratives of the Roman Empire under the Severans (2014)

people.name: Macrinus
people.summary: Mauretanian equestrian lawyer from Caesarea who had Caracalla killed and became the first emperor not of senatorial rank; he bought peace from Parthia after Nisibis and lost the throne to Elagabalus' supporters.
people.death: captured in Cappadocia and executed, June 218

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Elagabalus
people.fullName: Marcus Aurelius Antoninus (born Varius Avitus Bassianus)
people.summary: Teenage priest-emperor from Emesa who promoted his sun god Elagabal above Jupiter, married a Vestal, and scandalised Rome; murdered with his mother by the Praetorians.
people.detail: Ancient accounts of his sexual life, including a wish to be called empress, are now read partly as invective, though Dio is contemporary. The HA life is largely fantasy.
people.death: killed by the Praetorians with his mother Soaemias, March 222

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Julia Maesa
people.summary: Sister of Julia Domna and grandmother of Elagabalus and Severus Alexander; she organised the coup of 218 with her fortune and later engineered the replacement of Elagabalus by Alexander.
people.death: natural causes, c. 224; deified

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Julia Mamaea
people.summary: Mother and dominant adviser of Severus Alexander; she invited Origen to Antioch for theological discussion and was blamed by Herodian for her son's timidity and avarice. Killed with him in 235.
people.death: murdered with Severus Alexander near Mogontiacum, 235

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Severus Alexander
people.fullName: Marcus Aurelius Severus Alexander (born Bassianus Alexianus)
people.summary: Last Severan emperor, ruling from age 13 under his mother Mamaea and a council of senators; faced the new Sasanian threat and Germanic invasions and was murdered by his soldiers on the Rhine.
people.detail: The HA's idealised portrait (his household shrine with Christ, Abraham and Orpheus) is fiction, but the reign saw relative calm in government and law.
people.death: murdered by mutinous soldiers at Vicus Britannicus near Mogontiacum, March 235

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Artabanus IV
people.summary: Last Arsacid great king (often numbered V), who fought Macrinus to a bloody draw at Nisibis in 217 but was defeated and killed by Ardashir at Hormozgan in 224.
people.death: killed in battle at Hormozgan, 224

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Vologaeses V
people.summary: Arsacid king who backed Niger, besieged Nisibis in 197 and lost Ctesiphon to Severus' invasion of 197-198.

people.name: Ardashir I
people.summary: Founder of the Sasanian Empire; overthrew Artabanus IV in 224, built Ardashir-Khwarrah, attacked Roman Mesopotamia (230, 237-240) and captured Hatra with his son Shapur.
people.detail: Later Persian tradition (Karnamag-i Ardashir) made him a legendary hero and ideal king; the Testament of Ardashir circulated as a mirror for princes in Islamic times.
people.death: natural causes, c. 242

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Shapur I

roles.t: King of Kings of Iran and non-Iran

people.summary: The most successful foreign enemy of third-century Rome: he defeated Gordian III at Misiche (244), sacked Antioch, destroyed Dura and captured Valerian at Edessa (260), recording his deeds in the trilingual ŠKZ inscription and the rock reliefs of Naqsh-e Rustam and Bishapur.
people.detail: He settled Roman captives in new cities in Khuzestan and Persis, patronised Mani, and took the expanded title 'King of Kings of Iran and non-Iran' (Eran ud Aneran).
people.death: natural causes at Bishapur, c. 270-272
scholarship: Huyse, Die dreisprachige Inschrift Šābuhrs I. an der Ka'ba-i Zardušt (1999)
Canepa, The Two Eyes of the Earth (2009)

people.name: Maximinus Thrax
people.summary: A gigantic soldier of humble Balkan origin (the 'Thracian' label may be a slur), proclaimed by the Rhine army in 235; he campaigned deep into Germany (Harzhorn) and on the Danube but never visited Rome, and his fiscal exactions provoked the revolts of 238.
people.detail: Herodian and the HA present him as a barbarous peasant; in fact he had a long equestrian career. His reign is the conventional start of the soldier-emperors.
people.death: murdered by his own troops at the siege of Aquileia, 238

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Gordian I
people.summary: Octogenarian aristocratic proconsul of Africa proclaimed at Thysdrus in 238; after his son fell at Carthage he hanged himself, having reigned about three weeks.
people.death: suicide by hanging at Carthage, 238

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Gordian II
people.fullName: Marcus Antonius Gordianus Sempronianus Romanus Africanus
people.summary: Son and co-emperor of Gordian I, killed leading the Carthaginian militia against Capelianus' legion.
people.death: killed in battle outside Carthage, 238

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Pupienus
people.summary: Senior senator and soldier chosen by the Senate as co-emperor with Balbinus in 238; murdered by the Praetorians after 99 days.
people.death: killed by the Praetorians, 238

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Balbinus
people.summary: Patrician senator co-elected with Pupienus in 238; he governed Rome during street fighting while Pupienus went north, and was killed with him by the Praetorians.
people.death: killed by the Praetorians, 238

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Gordian III
people.summary: Grandson of Gordian I, emperor at 13; under his prefect and father-in-law Timesitheus he campaigned against Shapur I, winning at Rhesaina but dying after the defeat at Misiche in 244.
people.death: died in Mesopotamia early 244, from battle wounds (Persian version) or murdered (Roman version)

people.name: Timesitheus
people.summary: Career equestrian administrator, attested on inscriptions through a long series of procuratorships, whose daughter Tranquillina married Gordian III; as prefect he directed the Persian war until his death from illness in 243.
people.death: illness (possibly poisoned) in 243

people.name: Philip the Arab
people.summary: From Trachonitis in Arabia, he succeeded Gordian III, made a costly peace with Shapur, celebrated Rome's millennium in 248 and was defeated and killed by Decius near Verona.
people.detail: Later Christian tradition made him the first Christian emperor; most historians reject this. He founded Philippopolis (Shahba) in his homeland.
people.death: killed in battle near Verona, 249

people.name: Decius
people.summary: Pannonian senator from Budalia near Sirmium who took the name Trajan, ordered universal sacrifice (250), and became the first emperor killed by a foreign enemy, at Abritus against Cniva's Goths.
people.death: killed in battle at Abritus, June 251

people.name: Herennius Etruscus
people.summary: Elder son and co-emperor of Decius, killed by an arrow at Abritus shortly before his father.
people.death: killed in battle at Abritus, 251

people.name: Cniva
people.summary: Gothic leader who besieged Novae, defeated Decius at Beroe, took Philippopolis and destroyed the Roman army at Abritus in 251; known chiefly from Jordanes and Dexippus.

people.name: Trebonianus Gallus
people.summary: Governor proclaimed after Abritus who paid the Goths to leave; his reign saw plague and Persian invasion, and he was murdered by his troops when Aemilianus invaded Italy.
people.death: killed by his own soldiers at Interamna, 253

people.name: Aemilianus
people.summary: Moorish-born governor of Moesia who beat the Goths, was proclaimed emperor, overthrew Gallus and was himself murdered after about three months near Spoletium.
people.death: killed by his own troops near Spoletium, 253

people.name: Valerian
people.summary: Elderly aristocratic senator who took power in 253 and shared it with his son Gallienus; he persecuted the clergy (257-258) and was captured by Shapur I at Edessa in 260, dying in captivity.
people.death: died in Persian captivity at an unknown date

people.name: Gallienus
people.summary: Son of Valerian who held the core empire through fifteen years of invasions, secessions (Postumus, Palmyra) and usurpations; credited with a mobile cavalry force, excluding senators from army commands and ending the persecution.
people.detail: He was initiated at Eleusis, patronised Plotinus (who sought his support for a philosophers' city, Platonopolis, in Campania) and promoted a Hellenising revival in portraiture and coinage. Senatorial historiography and the HA vilified him as frivolous; modern historians (de Blois, Potter) see a resourceful ruler in impossible circumstances.
people.death: murdered by his officers outside Milan, September 268
scholarship: De Blois, The Policy of the Emperor Gallienus (1976)

people.name: Postumus
people.summary: Probably a Batavian, commander on the Rhine, who founded the Gallic Empire in 260 and defended Gaul, Britain and Spain for nine years without attempting to take Rome.
people.death: killed by his own troops at Mogontiacum after refusing them its sack, 269

people.name: Victorinus
people.summary: Praetorian prefect of Postumus who became Gallic emperor, sacked Augustodunum after a seven-month siege and was murdered at Cologne, reportedly by an officer whose wife he had seduced.
people.death: murdered at Colonia Agrippinensis, 271

people.name: Tetricus I
people.summary: Senatorial governor of Aquitania proclaimed Gallic emperor in 271 with the backing of Victorinus' mother Victoria; defeated by Aurelian at Châlons in 274, he walked in the triumph and was given an Italian governorship.

people.name: Odaenathus

roles.t: King of Kings; corrector totius Orientis

people.summary: Palmyrene noble and Roman senator who harried Shapur's army after Valerian's capture, crushed the Macriani's Quietus at Emesa, and led two counter-offensives to Ctesiphon as Gallienus' eastern commander.
people.death: assassinated at Emesa with his son Herodianus by a relative, Maeonius, 267

people.name: Zenobia
people.summary: Widow of Odaenathus, who ruled for her son Vaballathus and extended Palmyrene power over Egypt and most of Asia Minor (270-271) before defeat by Aurelian at Immae and Emesa and capture in 272.
people.detail: Ancient sources romanticised her as a chaste huntress-queen claiming descent from Cleopatra. Her end is variously told: death on the journey to Rome, or exhibition in Aurelian's triumph and retirement at Tibur, where descendants were known in the fourth century.

people.name: Vaballathus
people.fullName: Lucius Julius Aurelius Septimius Vaballathus Athenodorus
people.summary: Son of Odaenathus and Zenobia in whose name Palmyra ruled the East; his coins first paired him with Aurelian, then proclaimed him Augustus in 272.

people.name: Zabdas
people.summary: Zenobia's general who conquered Egypt in 270 and commanded at Immae and Emesa.

people.name: Claudius II Gothicus
people.summary: Illyrian officer who succeeded Gallienus after joining the plot against him; defeated the Alamanni at Lake Benacus and the Goths at Naissus, and died of plague at Sirmium.
people.detail: Constantine later claimed descent from him, so the HA and fourth-century sources inflate his virtues.
people.death: plague at Sirmium, 270

people.name: Quintillus
people.summary: Brother of Claudius II, recognised by the Senate on his death, but deserted when the army acclaimed Aurelian; died after a short reign, perhaps by suicide at Aquileia.
people.death: killed or suicide at Aquileia, 270

people.name: Aurelian
people.summary: Danubian cavalry general nicknamed 'manu ad ferrum' (hand on hilt) who in five years drove the Juthungi from Italy, reconquered Palmyra and the Gallic Empire, abandoned Dacia, walled Rome, reformed the coinage and established Sol Invictus as an imperial cult; titled Restitutor Orbis.
people.death: murdered by his officers at Caenophrurium, 275
scholarship: Watson, Aurelian and the Third Century (1999)

people.name: Tacitus
people.summary: Elderly emperor chosen after Aurelian's murder; the HA's claims of senatorial election and kinship with the historian are fiction. He campaigned against Gothic raiders in Asia Minor and died at Tyana.
people.death: illness or murder at Tyana, 276

people.name: Florianus
people.summary: Praetorian prefect and half-brother of Tacitus who seized power on his death; killed by his troops at Tarsus after about three months, facing Probus.
people.death: killed by his own troops at Tarsus, 276

people.name: Probus
people.summary: Born at Sirmium, he restored the Rhine and Gaul after the invasions of 275-276, crushed several usurpers, finished the Aurelian Walls and encouraged viticulture in the provinces; killed by his soldiers at Sirmium.
people.death: murdered by his soldiers at Sirmium, 282

people.name: Carus
people.summary: Probably from Narbo, he took power from Probus, made his sons Caesars, invaded Persia and took Ctesiphon, dying in his camp in 283, reportedly struck by lightning.
people.death: died in his camp beyond the Tigris, 283

people.name: Carinus
people.summary: Elder son of Carus who ruled the West; defeated the usurper Julianus at Verona but was murdered by his own officers during the battle of the Margus against Diocletian.
people.death: murdered by one of his officers at the Margus, 285

people.name: Numerian
people.summary: Younger son of Carus, a poet, who led the army back from Persia; found dead in his litter near Nicomedia, blamed on his father-in-law Aper.
people.death: died in his litter near Nicomedia, 284, probably murdered

people.name: Uranius Antoninus
people.fullName: Lucius Julius Aurelius Sulpicius Severus Uranius Antoninus
people.summary: Priest of Elagabal at Emesa who organised resistance to Shapur I and struck coins as emperor in 253-254.

people.name: Ingenuus
people.summary: Governor of Pannonia who claimed the purple after Valerian's capture (or in 258) and was defeated by Aureolus at Mursa.
people.death: killed or drowned himself after Mursa, 260

people.name: Aureolus
people.summary: Dacian-born ex-shepherd who led Gallienus' mobile cavalry, defeating Ingenuus and the Macriani, then rebelled at Milan in 268 in favour of Postumus and finally for himself.
people.death: surrendered to Claudius II and killed, 268

people.name: Dexippus

roles.t: Archon basileus and eponymous archon of Athens

people.summary: Athenian aristocrat, historian of the Gothic wars (Scythica) and a world Chronicle, who led Athenian resistance after the Herulian sack of 267/268; new fragments recovered from a Vienna palimpsest since 2014 have expanded his text.

people.name: Cyprian
people.summary: Wealthy rhetorician converted c. 246, bishop of Carthage through the Decian persecution, the plague that bears his name and the disputes over the lapsed and baptism; beheaded under Valerian.
people.detail: His De Unitate Ecclesiae, letters and councils made the African church a model of episcopal collegiality; his clash with Pope Stephen over rebaptism of heretics foreshadowed later Roman claims.
people.death: beheaded at Carthage, 14 September 258

people.name: Origen

roles.t: Head of the catechetical school of Alexandria

people.summary: Alexandrian Christian scholar, author of the Hexapla, the treatise On First Principles and Against Celsus, who taught at Caesarea after a break with his bishop; tortured in the Decian persecution, he died at Tyre around 253.
people.detail: His allegorical exegesis and speculative theology shaped Eastern thought; Eusebius was his admirer, but several of his doctrines were condemned in 553.
people.death: after torture under Decius, at Tyre, c. 253

people.name: Plotinus
people.summary: Founder of Neoplatonism, born in Egypt, who taught in Rome from 244 to 269 under the patronage of Gallienus and Salonina; his treatises were edited by his pupil Porphyry as the Enneads.
people.death: illness in Campania, 270

people.name: Cassius Longinus
people.summary: Platonist philosopher and critic, teacher of Porphyry at Athens, who became an adviser to Zenobia and was executed by Aurelian after Palmyra's fall.
people.death: executed by Aurelian at Emesa, 272 or 273

people.name: Paul of Samosata
people.summary: Bishop of Antioch condemned in 268 for teaching that Christ was a man indwelt by the Logos; his refusal to leave the church house led to Aurelian's ruling of 272.

people.name: Mani
people.summary: Babylonian prophet, raised among the Elchasaite baptists, who founded Manichaeism around 240, enjoyed Shapur I's favour, and died in prison under Bahram I.
people.death: died in chains at Bet Lapat, c. 274-277
scholarship: Gardner and Lieu, Manichaean Texts from the Roman Empire (2004)
